locations.name: The Corridor
locations.lede: Feels about a yard wide, just enough room to avoid a leg cramp but it is a full length of the train. And the only way from any berth to any other.

appearance.heading: Appearance
paragraphs: Windows down one side, doors down the other, and a runner of carpet that shows every step taken on it while the rain was falling.

why_it_matters.heading: Why It Matters
paragraphs: Nobody stays in the corridor. Everybody crosses it. Whoever was where, they were here first.

locations.name: The Dining Car
locations.lede: Eight tables, six of them laid, and a steward who remembers what everyone drinks without being told.

service.heading: Service
paragraphs: The last order is taken at half past nine and the car is dark by ten. Anyone still seated after that was not eating.

locations.name: The Guard's Van

locations.name: The Platform

why_it_matters.heading: Why It Matters

locations.name: The Vestibule

why_it_matters.heading: Why It Matters

articles.title: Lamps Found Extinguished End to End
articles.caption: The aisle after midnight, lamps cold.
articles.lede: The conductor, with a face of confusion, insisted the lamps were trimmed at eight.
body: Yet no passenger admits to having passed that way since, and the corridor now lies dark from vestibule to vestibule.
Our correspondent walked its length twice and met no one, which he notes is itself remarkable on a train carrying forty-one souls.
As the wind continued to howl, the conductor became increasingly agitated and emotional distraught.
Questions concerning the lamps are now met not with answers, but accusations, curses, and theories implicating nearly every demon aboard.

articles.title: Mysterious Woman Seen Walking the Aisle
articles.caption: The aisle of Car No. 7, looking forward.
articles.lede: Railway employees report unusual activity shortly after midnight, and the steward is unable to account for a second setting laid at table nine.
body: The steward maintains that the fourth chair was drawn out before the soup, and that no one sat in it.
> "I did not lay it," he told our correspondent. "But the chair was drawn out before the soup came, as though someone had already taken her seat."
A porter questioned afterward disputed the steward’s account, but became visibly uneasy when asked whether he had seen anyone in the aisle.
> "I saw somebody," he said. "That is not the same thing."
He would say no more.

Several passengers later reported seeing a woman walking alone toward the forward vestibule shortly after midnight. No description agrees beyond this: she wore dark clothing, moved without haste, and was not seen returning.
Passengers were thereafter asked to remain in their compartments until the border and to report any door found unlocked that ought not to have been.

articles.title: The Continental Express Departs Under Cover of Rain
articles.caption: The platform, moments before departure.
articles.lede: The Continental Express departed through a hard evening rain, the platform heavy with the smell of wet timber, musky tobacco, coal smoke, and hot iron. Glisening, the lamps were already burning against the weather and the station nearly deserted by the time the last whistle sounded.
body: Boarding was otherwise without incident, save for two small irregularities which railway officials have thus far been unable to explain: one berth appears to have been claimed by two passengers, while a trunk was found aboard which no porter remembers carrying. Our correspondent, travelling in Car No. 7, observed the guard make two complete examinations of the train after departure. On the second occasion he was heard asking a steward, in some irritation,
> "Then where is the other one?"
The steward gave no answer within our hearing.

At the last halt, the stationmaster declined to discuss the matter and ordered the platform cleared before the train resumed its journey. Railway officials continue their enquiries. Any passenger possessing knowledge of the disputed berth, the unidentified luggage, or the person to whom either may belong is requested to present themselves to the conductor before the border crossing.
Passengers boarded without incident, though the guard reports one berth claimed twice and a trunk no porter admits to carrying.

Our correspondent, travelling in Car No. 7, reports that the guard has twice walked the length of the train without satisfying himself as to the whereabouts of the missing party. The stationmaster at the last halt declined to comment.
Enquiries continue. Any passenger with knowledge of the affair is asked to present themselves at the conductor's office before the border crossing.

articles.title: The Whole Carriage Circled by Our Photographer
articles.caption: The carriage, circled at speed.
articles.lede: A circuit of the carriage made from the trackside disclosed several particulars not apparent from within.
body: One window stood unlatched. Beneath it, on the rain-darkened paintwork, our photographer found the distinct mark of a hand. Farther along, a lamp still burned behind the curtain of a berth whose occupant insisted it had been extinguished before midnight.
A full turn about the coach reveals a window unlatched from within and a lamp still burning in a berth its occupant swears was dark.
From the trackside the coach gives up what its corridors hide: one window unlatched, and the mark of a hand below it on the paintwork.
The railway declines to say whether the train was stopped between halts. Our photographer, who was standing beside it, says it was.

articles.title: Near Wall Removed: The Compartments Laid Bare
articles.caption: Car No. 7 in section, near wall removed.
articles.lede: With the trackside wall cut away, every compartment can be read at once. Our readers are invited to draw their own conclusions.
body: Presented in section, the coach reads as a row of small rooms, each with its own account of the night, and no two accounts agreeing.
The Gazette offers no verdict. It offers the plan of the carriage, the hour of each movement, and the names of those aboard.

paragraphs: Railway property again, in a train full of it. The guard turns them down at ten and does not count them, because in thirty years there has never been a reason to.

items.name: Hand Axe
items.lede: Short-hafted, single-bitted, and the one thing in the van that has an honest reason to be there: a crate is opened with an axe or it is not opened.

the_bit.heading: The Bit
paragraphs: Bright along the edge and dulled at the heel, which is wear from prying rather than from cutting.

the_haft.heading: The Haft
paragraphs: Wrapped where a hand goes, and the wrapping is newer than the wear under it.

provenance.heading: Provenance
paragraphs: Railway tool or the Order's, depending on who is asked, and the two answers have been given by two people about the same axe.

items.name: Escort's Dagger
items.lede: Plain, short, and issued rather than chosen: one of four the same, worn under the cloak where a coat would hide it.

the_blade.heading: The Blade
paragraphs: No maker's mark and no ornament. The Order does not commission, it equips, and what it equips is the cheapest thing that will do the work.

the_sheath.heading: The Sheath
paragraphs: Sewn to the belt rather than hung from it, which is how a thing is carried by somebody expecting to need it in a corridor.

provenance.heading: Provenance
paragraphs: Not on the manifest. Nothing the escort carries is on the manifest, and the warrant is why nobody at Calais asked.

items.name: War Hammer
items.lede: A head of steel on a short haft, weighted so far forward that it is useless for anything except what it is for.

the_head.heading: The Head
paragraphs: Faced on one side and spiked on the other, and the spike has been ground back to a stub by somebody who wanted it to look like a mallet.

why_it_is_aboard.heading: Why It Is Aboard
paragraphs: Nobody has offered a reason. Dame Marchand answers questions about the cargo with the same sentence each time, and this is not the cargo.

provenance.heading: Provenance
paragraphs: Under the same warrant as the rest, sealed in wax that is not any nation's.

items.name: Arming Sword
items.lede: A yard of straight steel, which is a yard more than the width of the corridor it would have to be swung in.

the_blade.heading: The Blade
paragraphs: Sharpened along its whole length and lately, by somebody who did the work in a hurry and left the stone's grit in the fuller.

where_it_was.heading: Where It Was
paragraphs: Racked in the guard's van with three others, in a stand made for four. The leather at one station is compressed and at the rest it is not.

provenance.heading: Provenance
paragraphs: The Order's, under warrant, and the only weapon aboard that could not be concealed by anybody carrying it anywhere.

items.name: Bottle of Laudanum
items.lede: Tincture of opium, dispensed in Vienna, in a brown bottle with a measure marked down the side.

the_measure.heading: The Measure
paragraphs: The book in the doctor's bag records what was poured and when. The bottle is three doses lighter than the book has an entry for.

who_it_is_for.heading: Who It Is For
paragraphs: The label carries a name that is not Dr. Weiss's and not any name on the passenger list, in handwriting that is his.

provenance.heading: Provenance
paragraphs: Declared at Calais as medical, which it is, and which is the reason nobody looked at how much of it there was.

items.name: Luggage Strap
items.lede: Six feet of harness leather with a brass buckle, of which the guard's van holds a dozen and the register accounts for eleven.

the_leather.heading: The Leather
paragraphs: Stretched along one section and nowhere else, the way leather goes when it has been pulled hard once rather than loaded often.

where_they_hang.heading: Where They Hang
paragraphs: On a rail inside the van door, in a row, and the gap in the row is not at the end where a man reaching in a hurry would take one from.

provenance.heading: Provenance
paragraphs: Railway property, unremarkable, and the only thing aboard that could kill a man without anybody having brought it.

items.name: Ornate Dagger
items.lede: A hand's length of blade, chased along the spine and fitted to a sheath it is no longer in. Both are on the floor of the van, a foot apart, past the crates and under the window, where the light does not reach.

the_blade.heading: The Blade
paragraphs: Ornamental, and sharpened anyway. The chasing runs to the edge and stops, the way a maker's work does when the edge is meant to be honed and the pattern is not meant to be worn away.
It has been wiped. Not cleaned -- wiped, once, along one face, by somebody in more of a hurry than the wiping was worth.

the_sheath.heading: The Sheath
paragraphs: Lying open and empty, which is the part worth reading. A dagger dropped in a struggle keeps its sheath on a belt. A dagger drawn somewhere else and carried here arrives with the sheath in the other hand.

provenance.heading: Provenance
paragraphs: Nothing on the manifest matches it, and nothing in the van was opened to let it out. It came aboard in somebody's luggage and left that luggage before the border.

items.name: Pocket Watch
items.lede: Silver, stopped, and running eleven minutes behind the carriage clock when last it ran.
body: The case holds a portrait that has been cut down to fit, and cut badly.

items.name: Service Revolver
items.lede: Webley, service issue, and older than the marriage it came into. Carried in a travelling case fitted for it, which is not how a keepsake is carried.

the_cylinder.heading: The Cylinder
paragraphs: Six chambers, five loaded. The sixth has been fired and not cleaned since, and the fouling is old enough to be about some other evening entirely.

the_case.heading: The Case
paragraphs: Lined in green baize with a recess cut for the revolver and a second recess, the same size, cut for something that is not in it.

provenance.heading: Provenance
paragraphs: Sir Rupert's, entered on no declaration at Calais. Lady Beaumont says she did not know it was in the luggage, and knows which case it is in.

items.name: Telegram
items.lede: Handed aboard at Paris, folded twice, and addressed to a name that is not the one M. Dupont travels under.

text.heading: Text
paragraphs: It reads, in full: DO NOT DINE AT NINE.

provenance.heading: Provenance
paragraphs: Filed at Paris at half past three, an hour before the train left, by a sender the clerk recorded only as "a lady".
bullets: Filed 15:30, Paris
No sender name on the counterfoil
Delivered to the carriage, not the platform office

items.name: Train Ticket
items.lede: Continental Express, Calais to the border, berth 4 of Car No. 7.
body: The clerk's hand has corrected the berth number once, and the correction is initialled by nobody.

notices.title: Goblins Are Banned
notices.lede: The strip is printed in the red the Gazette keeps for losses and warnings, which is the Order's way of saying this one is not a formality.

the_rule.heading: The Rule
paragraphs: Goblins are banned from the Northern Line. They will be slain by law, and the Order is held blameless in the carrying out of it.

what_nobody_says.heading: What Nobody Says
paragraphs: No clause explains how a guard is to tell. In practice the question is settled by whoever is holding the lamp.

notices.title: Notice to Passengers
notices.lede: The full posting, by order of the Knights of the Northern Line, in the frame every carriage carries beside the third window.

the_clauses.heading: The Clauses
bullets: Elves not allowed without permits.
Goblins are banned, and will be slain by law.
The rear cars are reserved for the older bloods and are locked between stations.
The Order's word is the record, and the record is not open to reading.

what_nobody_says.heading: What Nobody Says
paragraphs: The fourth clause is the one that matters. Everything the other three claim rests on a record no passenger is permitted to check.

notices.title: Elves Not Allowed Without Permits
notices.lede: Posted at Aldermoor and pasted in every carriage before the train left the platform.

the_rule.heading: The Rule
paragraphs: Permits are issued at Aldermoor and nowhere else on this line. A permit names one journey, one direction, and one carriage, and the guard is entitled to ask for it at any point between stations.

what_nobody_says.heading: What Nobody Says
paragraphs: The permit office at Aldermoor keeps no evening hours. Anyone who boards after dark boards without one.
